Unusual presentation of stiff- person syndrome in a 
patient with type 1 diabetes mellitus
Bala Munipalli, Jaimin S Shah 
Case report

SUMMARY
Stiff-
 person syndrome (SPS) is a r
are, autoimmune, 
neurological disorder that often occurs concurrently with 
other autoimmune disorders, such as type 1 diabetes 
mellitus, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and Hashimoto’s 
thyroiditis. It also can manifest as a paraneoplastic 
syndrome. Although SPS classically presents with truncal 
and appendicular stiffness and lumbar hyperlordosis, 
it can present focally in a single limb (termed stiff-

limb 
syndrome). Here, we describe a woman with stiff-
 limb 
syndrome who initially presented with concerns about 
right foot swelling and pain.
 She also was positive for 
anti-
 GAD65 (anti-
 GAD2) antibodies
. With treatment, 
she regained the ability to drive and ambulate without 
a walker, and she had a noted reduction in stimulus-

induced spasms
.
BACKGROUND
Stiff- person syndrome (SPS; previously termed 
stiff
-

man syndrome) is a rare, autoimmune, neuro-
logical disorder that often occurs concurrently 
with other autoimmune disorders, such as type 1 
diabetes mellitus, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and 
Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. It also can manifest as a 
paraneoplastic syndrome and may be associated 
with antibodies against glutamate decarboxylase 
2 (GAD2; also termed GAD65) or amphiphysin. 
Although SPS classically presents with muscular 
rigidity and spasm affecting the truncal and appen-
dicular muscles, it can present focally in a single 
limb (termed stiff-

limb syndrome).1 Although SPS is 
a rare disorder, it may be first observed by a primary 
care provider or general internist. Early recogni-
tion of SPS and its variants is important to prevent 
delays in care because delays are associated with an 
increased risk of aspiration, respiratory arrest and 
autonomic dysfunction, resulting in sudden death.
2
CASE PRESENTATION
The patient was a woman in her early 40 s. She had 
a 
20-
 year history
 of type 1 diabetes mellitus and a 
10-
 year history of r
heumatoid arthritis; she also had 
vitiligo and Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. She presented 
with an 8-
 month
 history of right ankle stiffness and 
described periodic spasms of knee extension and 
ankle plantar flexion that could be triggered by 
sudden noise or movement. She had repeated falls, 
including one in the shower, that prompted reliance 
on a walker. She was unable to drive her car because 
of stiffness in her right leg. She also thought that 
her foot was swelling and noted intermittent viola-
ceous discolouration.
These symptoms resulted in her visiting her local 
emergency department, and she subsequently was 
seen by multiple specialists. An evaluation for deep 
venous thrombosis was negative. Empiric antibiotic 
treatment for cellulitis and trials of compression 
stockings and physiotherapy for suspected lymph-
edema were not helpful. Multiple imaging tests of 
the right lower extremity, including MRI studies 
and plain radiographs, showed no relevant abnor -
malities. A consultation with a neurologist yielded 
no definitive diagnosis after electromyography, 
and nerve conduction studies were interpreted as 
showing normal results. She then came to our insti-
tution for additional evaluation.
INVESTIGATIONS
Our examination was notable for board-  like stiff-
ness of the right ankle, with a complete inability 
to passively dorsiflex or plantar flex the ankle 
(video

1). Mild stiffness was observed in her right 
knee. Her muscle tone was normal in the bilateral 
upper and left lower extremity, and the passive 
range of motion was normal. She did not have 
truncal stiffness or hyperlordosis. Her muscle bulk 
was normal, sensation testing showed intact percep-
tion of light touch, pinprick, vibration and proprio-
ception, and she had normal finger-
 to-
 nose test 
results. W
ith a casual gait, she had minimal move-
ment of the right ankle, causing the absence of a 
normal heel strike. She was unable to walk on the 
toes of her right foot (video

1). The remainder of 
her neurologic examination findings were normal. 
Her gastrocnemius and tibialis anterior muscles felt 
firm and taut to palpation and were without any 
oedema or discolouration. She had vitiligo patches 
on her upper extremities, particularly her hands.
Laboratory evaluations showed elevated levels 
of serum anti-
 GAD65 antibody (185
 nmol/L; refer-
ence range,<0.02
 nmol/L), thyro
globulin antibody 
(171
 IU/mL; reference range,<4.0
 IU/mL), and 
thyroid pero
xidase antibody (85.9
 IU/mL; 
refer-
ence range,<9.0
 IU/mL). Needle electromyography 
(performed 
by J.S.S.) showed continuous motor unit 
activity that was present with attempted relaxation, 
most prominently in the distal right leg muscles.
DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS
The presentation of firm and taut musculature in 
the right distal leg, in combination with the patient’s 
perception of swelling, pain and discolouration, 
prompted unnecessary evaluations and laboratory 
tests for cellulitis, lymphedema and other ortho-
paedic and vascular problems, thereby delaying the 
diagnosis. However, the patient’s history of multiple

autoimmune disorders, including type 1 diabetes mellitus, 
thyroiditis and vitiligo, raised clinical suspicion for GAD65-

associated autoimmunity
. Episodic spasms that were precipitated 
by sudden noise or movement and recurrent falls were important 
historical details because these are cardinal features of SPS. The 
lack of response to therapies such as compression stockings, 
physiotherapy (for presumed lymphedema) and antibiotics (for 
presumed cellulitis), along with multiple negative diagnostic 
test results, helped exclude other contributing diagnoses. A 
serum anti-
 GAD65 antibody level 
greater than 100
 nmol/L 
and 
needle electromyography results showing continuous motor unit 
activity with attempted relaxation provided supporting evidence 
of SPS.
TREATMENT
The patient was treated with diazepam 5 mg three times per day . 
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) was loaded at a dose of 2
 g/
kg total body 
weight, divided over 5
 days followed by a mainte
-
nance regimen of 1
 g/kg, divided over 2
 days, every 4
 weeks.
OUTCOME AND FOLLOW-UP
After 3 months of follow-  up, she had completed three total 
cycles of IVIg. She regained the ability to drive and ambulate 
without a walker, and she had a noted reduction in stimulus-

induced spasms. Although she continued to have significant 
stiffness of the right ankle, 
she was able to walk with a normal 
heel strike (video

2).
DISCUSSION
SPS is a rare disorder that presents with muscular rigidity and 
episodic spasms, primarily of appendicular and axial muscles.3–5 
It was first described in 1956 by Moersch and Woltman, 6 and 
it has an estimated prevalence of 1 or 2 cases per million, 
with an incidence of 1 case per million per year.
3 Women are 
affected 2 to 3 times more often than men, and most patients 
are aged 20–50 years at the time of diagnosis.
7 It rarely occurs 
in childhood. Classically, SPS predominantly involves paraspinal, 
abdominal wall and proximal lower limb muscles symmetrically. 
Involved muscles frequently are firm and taut, and hypertonia 
generally does not have the classic clinical features of parkin-
sonian rigidity or spasticity. Another common finding is fixed 
spinal hyperlordosis that does not improve when lying supine 
or with forward flexion of the spine. As observed with this 
patient, SPS may also have an asymmetric or focal presentation, 
including involvement isolated to unilateral or bilateral upper 
or lower extremities (stiff-
 limb syndrome) 
or isolated to axial 
muscles (stiff-
 trunk syndrome). 
Progressive encephalomyelitis 
with rigidity and myoclonus, a more fulminant SPS-
 like 
disorder, 
presents with more severe and widespread muscle hypertonia, 
oculobulbar dysfunction, dysautonomia, myelopathy and 
encephalopathy.
1 Antibodies against GAD65 are identified in as 
many as 80% of patients with SPS. Antibodies against the α1 
subunit of the glycine receptor (GlyRα1) may be identified in 
as many as 25% of patients who are seronegative for GAD65. 
Antibodies against amphiphysin may be found in patients with 
an SPS-
 like 
disorder associated with breast adenocarcinoma or 
small-
 cell lung cancer
.8
GABAergic pathways (involving γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) 
secretion or transmission) are the primary target of autoim-
munity in SPS. Although anti-
 GAD65 
antibodies are a marker 
of SPS, 9 they are unlikely to be directly pathogenic. GAD65 
is an intracellular cytoplasmic protein, and antibodies directed 
against cytoplasmic targets generally implicate primarily 
cytotoxic T cell-
 mediated autoimmunity
.10 When present, 
serum anti-
 GAD65 antibody concentrations typically ex
ceed 
100
 nmol/L in patients with SPS, and at these concentrations,

they can help confirm the diagnosis. Values less than 20
 nmol/L

are less diagnostically specific and may be identified in 8% of 
the general population and in patients with type 1 diabetes 
without SPS. Anti-
 GAD65 antibodies are associated with other

autoimmune neurologic syndromes, including cerebellar ataxia, 
myelopathy, autoimmune encephalitis, autonomic neurop-
athy and large-
 fibre peripheral neuropathy
.11 One or more 
systemic autoimmune disorders frequently accompany GAD65-  
associated autoimmune neurologic disorders, including autoim
-
mune thyroiditis, pernicious anaemia, type 1 diabetes mellitus 
and vitiligo.
GABAergic medications diazepam and baclofen may be used 
for initial symptomatic treatment. Diazepam is usually initiated 
at 5
 mg, 2–3 times per day
, but a total daily dose of 40
 mg/day 
or greater 
is frequently needed for adequate symptom control. 9 
Baclofen may be started at 10
 mg, 
3–4 times per day, and grad-
ually increased to a maximum of 80
 mg/day
. Sedation is the 
most common dose-
 limiting adverse effect 
for both agents, but 
patients with SPS frequently are able to tolerate higher doses 
with gradual titration. Intrathecal baclofen can be highly effec-
tive for patients with refractory disease and when titration of 
oral medication is poorly tolerated.

right lower extremity. When walking, she did not have a normal heel 
strike.
Video 2 F ollow-  up ev aluation. After 3 months of therapy, she had a 
normal heel strike when walking.

For most patients, immunotherapy should be initiated early 
and administered concurrently with symptomatic therapies. 
Early initiation of immunotherapy may be associated with better 
outcomes than delayed initiation. Acutely symptomatic patients 
may begin treatment with IVIg (2
 g/kg divided over 
3–5
 days, 
followed by 1
 g/kg given over 1–2
 days and repeated monthly 
as 
maintenance therapy). A randomised blinded crossover trial 
reported that 11 of 16 patients with SPS had improvement in 
multiple functional measures and had fewer falls with IVIg versus 
placebo.
12 Intravenous methylprednisolone may be used in a 
similar manner (1000
 mg/day for 3–5 consecutive days, repeated 
weekly 
for 2–3 months). Rituximab and cyclophosphamide may 
be considered for patients with refractory disease. Patients may 
be transitioned to an oral immunosuppressant (eg, azathioprine, 
mycophenolate mofetil) for maintenance therapy.

Patient’s perspective
I am feeling a little more secure on my feet. Still a slight ‘drag’ 
of my right foot, but only a few trips. No falls. I am using the 
walker for extended periods of movement, but nothing for short 
distances. I have been taking (diazepam) about an hour prior to 
driving. The fact that I am driving, shows improvement there! 
Depending on the length of my workday or length of drive time, 
sometimes I take another one in the evening. I believe I am 
averaging 30 pills every 20 days.
Learning points
 ► Stiff- person syndrome is an autoimmune neurologic disorder 
that is characterised by fluctuating muscular rigidity and may 
present with either generalised and symmetric axial and limb 
muscle involvement or focal and asymmetric involvement of a 
single limb (stiff-
 limb syndrome).
 ► Stiff- person syndrome (SPS) is associated with serum 
anti-
 glutamate decarboxylase 2 (anti-
 GAD65) antibodies 
in excess of 100
 nmol/L and frequently occurs with other 
systemic autoimmune disorders
, including type 1 diabetes, 
autoimmune thyroiditis and pernicious anaemia.
 ► Primary care physicians should have a high index of 
suspicion for SPS and other GAD65-
 related autoimmune 
neurologic disorders in patients with type 1 diabetes and 
other GAD65-
 associated systemic autoimmune disorders 
to avoid unnecessary medical care and delayed initiation 
of immunotherapy,
 which has been associated with poorer 
outcomes.
